body.hook: Big tech companies watch real people use their products before launch, often finding problems the designers never imagined. The rule is simple: you are not your user. Today you plan how to watch real users try your product.

study.title: Test Plan
study.question: How do I find out whether real users can use my product?
study.passage:
User-test plan (written for this lesson):
1. Goal: What do you want to learn? Example: "Can Grade 8 students add a homework task and find tomorrow's tasks without help?"
2. Testers: Choose five users who match your problem statement, not just friends from your team.
3. Tasks: Write three tasks in plain words without giving away the steps. Good: "Add your science homework due Friday." Bad: "Tap the plus button, then type science."
4. Measures: For each task record whether it was completed (yes/no), time taken, number of mistakes and what the user said (think-aloud).
5. Script: Welcome the tester; explain you are testing the product, not them; ask them to think aloud; don't help unless they are completely stuck; thank them.
6. After-test questions: "What was easiest? What was confusing? Would you use this? Why or why not?"

body.hook: You've watched five people use your product. Now you have pages of notes, times and quotes. The hard part isn't collecting feedback; it's figuring out what it means and what to do first.

study.title: Make Sense of Feedback
study.question: What do my user-test results tell me?
study.passage:
Sample results (written for this lesson), homework app, five testers:
Task 1, Add homework due Friday: 5 of 5 completed; average time 25 seconds; 2 testers first tapped the title instead of "+."
Task 2, Find tomorrow's homework: 2 of 5 completed; average time 70 seconds; 3 testers said "Where's the calendar?"
Task 3, Delete a finished task: 4 of 5 completed; 1 tester said "I'm scared I'll delete the wrong one."
After-test comments: "I like how fast it is." "The text is tiny on my phone." "I'd use it if it reminded me at night."
Steps: 1. Calculate the success rate for each task. 2. Write each observation on a sticky note and group them into themes (affinity map). 3. Rate each problem's severity: 3 = stops users finishing a task, 2 = slows or confuses users, 1 = small annoyance. 4. List the top three problems to fix.

body.objective: Students will be able to make quality improvements.
successCriteria: I can make quality improvements based on user-test results
I can retest to check improvements worked

body.hook: Users rarely notice good design, but they always notice bad design. Fixing the top problems from testing turns a product that "kind of works" into one people actually want to use.

Making a product available to users.

study.title: Quality Pass
study.question: How do I make my product good enough to release?
study.passage:
Quality improvement plan (written for this lesson):
1. Fix the top three problems from user testing. Example fixes for the homework app: add a "Tomorrow" button on the home screen (Task 2 problem); increase text to at least 16 point (tiny text); add an "Are you sure?" message before deleting (delete fear).
2. Retest the same tasks with three new testers. Compare success rates and times before and after.
3. Quality checklist before release: All MVP features work. No known severity-3 bugs. Text is readable on a phone. Buttons are big enough to tap (about 1 cm). Colour is not the only way information is shown (for colour-blind users). Spelling and grammar are correct. The product solves the problem statement.
4. Decide: ready to release, or another iteration?
